sections.heading: AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust

content.text: When does an AI assistant improve human decision-making, and when does it hurt? We argue that the answer depends not just on AI accuracy but also on how much its evidence overlaps with the human’s and how the human combines the two. A worker makes a binary decision by observing her own signal and receiving a recommendation from an AI. We develop a human behavioral model with two primitives: her awareness of the overlap and her trust in the AI. Our analysis gives a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability and overlap, with regions of complementarity, impairment, and automation. A worker who neglects the overlap (correlation neglect) can be made less accurate by a more capable AI, double-counting the shared evidence. Trust reshapes the regions - undertrust may compensate for correlation neglect, so that the trust level maximizing accuracy depends on the deployment parameters. Empirically, we identify the two model parameters by pairing the same workers with different AIs, and break the accuracy loss into a correlation-neglect cost and an undertrust cost, one tied to reducing overlap on the AI side, the other to calibrating trust on the human side. On ChatBench, AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 points, yet workers apply only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to AI information; GPT-4o falls in the automation region and Llama-3.1-8b stays at the complementarity boundary; and calibrating trust recovers about 2.6 points for GPT-4o but almost nothing for Llama-3.1-8b.

Empirical evaluations of human-AI teams reach very different conclusions. Some studies report large accuracy gains from AI assistance ([Tschandl et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib11); [Steyvers et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib2)), while many find no improvement over the unaided human, or outright degradation: a more capable AI can hurt team performance ([Bansal et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib8)), AI explanations need not help ([Bansal et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib9)), AI predictions may not improve expert radiologists ([Agarwal et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib12)), and a meta-analysis across tasks and systems finds that human-AI teams on average perform worse ([Vaccaro et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib7)). We argue that whether assistance helps turns not on the AI’s accuracy alone, but also on how much its evidence overlaps the human’s and on how the human combines it with her own. For example, when a worker treats overlapping evidence as if it were independent, she counts the shared part twice, a bias documented as correlation neglect in belief formation ([Enke and Zimmermann, 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib4); [Eyster and Weizsacker, 2010](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib1)), and the team can end up less accurate than the worker alone. This paper constructs a model built on these factors, uses it to characterize when AI assistance helps and when it hurts, and develops an empirical estimation strategy that exploits variation of outputs obtained by pairing the same workers with different AIs.

We study a binary classification problem in which the human and the AI each hold evidence about the state, summarized by their log-likelihood ratios ℓH\ell\_{H} and ℓA\ell\_{A}, and the worker decides by the sign of a weighted sum wH​ℓH+wA​ℓAw\_{H}\ell\_{H}+w\_{A}\ell\_{A}. The model has two parts. In the *observation model*, each agent’s evidence is a collection of *cues*, and the key primitive is the *overlap coefficient* λ\lambda, the share of the AI’s cues the human already holds. In the *behavioral model*, the worker combines the two signals through correlation awareness α^∈[0,1]\hat{\alpha}\in[0,1], representing how well she accounts for that overlap, and trust β^>0\hat{\beta}>0, how much weight she puts on the AI information. Two benchmarks sit inside this family. The *Bayes-rational* worker (α^=1,β^=1\hat{\alpha}=1,\hat{\beta}=1) de-correlates and weights optimally, while the *correlation-neglect* worker (α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0) treats the two signals as independent. Overlap is a property of the information, awareness and trust are properties of the worker, and together they determine the team’s accuracy.

Our first results compare team performance against human and AI alone. Under the Bayes-rational benchmark the team is at least as accurate as either source alone, and strictly more accurate unless the AI’s evidence already contains the human’s. The impairment and automation outcomes seen in the literature, outside that case, must then come from the worker’s behavior rather than from the information structure. Away from that benchmark, we obtain a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability τA\tau\_{A} and overlap λ\lambda with three regions, complementarity where the team is most accurate, impairment where the unaided human is, and automation where the AI alone is. Two of its features run against intuition. The first is that a more capable AI can make the team less accurate. When overlap is high (λ>1−β^/2\lambda>1-\hat{\beta}/2), a stronger AI only gives a correlation-neglecting worker more evidence to double-count, and that can lower accuracy. The second is that undertrust is not simply an error to be corrected. Reducing trust shrinks the impairment region but brings automation on at lower capability, so the trust level that maximizes team accuracy is not always β^=1\hat{\beta}=1 but depends on the deployment parameters.

Our second set of results turns the model into a measurement tool. A Bayes-rational worker’s weight on the AI changes with overlap, while a correlation-neglecting worker’s does not, and this difference lets us estimate the parameters by pairing the same workers with two AIs of different overlap. Trust β^\hat{\beta} is sharply identified, while awareness α^\hat{\alpha} is only weakly identified because the overlap coefficient in our experiment is relatively small. We then split the worker’s accuracy loss against the Bayes-rational benchmark into two parts that add up exactly at any level of awareness, a correlation-neglect cost from misperceiving the overlap and an undertrust cost from underweighting the AI. Each is tied to a distinct lever on opposite sides of the information-behavior divide: reducing overlap on the AI side by training it to supply what the human lacks, and calibrating trust on the human side.

We examine the framework in the context of ChatBench ([Chang et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib6)), where 643 workers answer multiple-choice questions paired with either GPT-4o or Llama-3.1-8b. AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 percentage points, yet workers put only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight on the AI (β^=0.285\hat{\beta}=0.285). GPT-4o is more capable and overlaps the human less, so it lies in the automation regime, where the AI alone beats the team; Llama-3.1-8b is weaker and overlaps more, so it sits at the boundary between complementarity and automation. The worker’s behavior is nearly the same in both, so it is the difference in AI capability between the two deployments that shifts the deployment from one regime to the other, as the framework predicts. The cost of undertrust is therefore uneven. We simulate a trust-calibrated decision rule, which recovers about 2.62.6 points accuracy for the strong AI and moves the team toward the boundary, but almost nothing for the weak AI.

The two sides of the information-behavior divide provide two design levers. On the human side, trust should be set to the deployment’s accuracy-maximizing level, not reflexively to β^=1\hat{\beta}=1, since some undertrust is protective in the impairment region. On the AI side, reducing overlap by training the AI to supply what the human lacks rather than what she already knows can raise team accuracy even without raising the AI’s own accuracy. The phase diagram also says when to show the AI at all: withhold its signal when the AI is too weak, provide it in the complementarity band, and automate once the AI is strong enough.

Our work sits among several literatures but differs in what it treats as endogenous. Studies of optimal human-AI collaboration through sufficient statistics ([Agarwal et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib3)) leave out the conditionally dependent signals that are central here. Work on reducing overreliance ([Buçinca et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib10)) and on testing whether AI adds to human expertise ([Alur et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib19); [Alur et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib20)) takes the intervention or the test as given, whereas we characterize the best deployment as a function of capability, overlap, and behavior. Closest in spirit, [Guo et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib21) define over- and under-reliance from the human’s adoption or switch rates against a Bayesian benchmark; our two parameters give a micro-foundation for their two sources of loss, trust for their reliance loss and correlation awareness for their discrimination loss, with a model of a worker who combines a continuous AI signal with her own rather than choosing per instance between the two recommendations. Other work on combining expert information ([Donahue et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib13); [Peng et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib14)) and learning-to-defer ([Madras et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib15); [Mozannar and Sontag, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib16); [Verma et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib17); [Wilder et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib18)) takes the human’s decision rule as exogenous, whereas we derive it from behavioral primitives. Section [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2 "2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") introduces the model, Section [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3 "3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") develops the phase diagram and welfare decomposition, and Section [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S4 "4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") presents the empirical framework and results.

A worker forms a tentative answer to a question, sees an AI assistant’s recommendation, and decides whether to revise. The evidence available about a question is a collection of *cues*, atomic units of evidence about the underlying answer that an agent might or might not access. For a question on classical mechanics, the cues are the relevant physical principles, the diagnostic features of the answer choices, and the patterns from prior similar problems. If a human and an AI both lean on the standard textbook derivation, there will be substantial overlap in cues whereas if they each approach the question through different reasoning paths there will be little overlap.

Formally, a binary state Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\} is drawn from the symmetric prior P⁡(Y=1)=P⁡(Y=0)=1/2P(Y=1)=P(Y=0)=1/2.11 1 We assume symmetric prior in the main text for simplicity. Appendix [F](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A6 "Appendix F Asymmetric Priors ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") describes an asymmetric prior extension with the main results and insights. There is a finite collection of NN cues {X1,…,XN}\{X\_{1},\ldots,X\_{N}\}, conditionally independent given YY:

We denote the *per-cue capability* by θ:=(μ1−μ0)2/(2​σ2)\theta:=(\mu\_{1}-\mu\_{0})^{2}/(2\sigma^{2}), the signal-to-noise ratio of a single cue. 22 2 Our results generalize to heterogeneous cues; see Appendix [E](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A5 "Appendix E Generalization of the cue-pool construction ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") for details.

The *capability* τB\tau\_{B} measures how informative agent BB’s evidence is. An agent who classifies via 𝟏{ℓB>0}\mathbf{1}\{\ell\_{B}>0\} is correct iff ℓB\ell\_{B} shares the sign of (2​Y−1)(2Y-1); by symmetry, this happens with probability Φ⁡(τB/2)\Phi(\sqrt{\tau\_{B}/2}), where Φ\Phi is the standard normal CDF. Standalone classification accuracy is thus Φ\Phi evaluated at the SNR, and is strictly increasing in τB\tau\_{B}.

We refer to the cue pool {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\} as the *domain* (a property of the question type), and to 𝒳H\mathcal{X}\_{H} as the human’s *access* within that domain. The following shows that, under uniform sampling, overlap depends on the domain and the human’s access but not on the AI’s capability.

Fix 𝒳H\mathcal{X}\_{H} with |𝒳H|=nH|\mathcal{X}\_{H}|=n\_{H}. Suppose the AI’s cue access 𝒳A\mathcal{X}\_{A} is a uniformly random subset of size nAn\_{A} drawn without replacement from {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\}. Then 𝔼⁡[λ]=nH/N\mathbb{E}[\lambda]=n\_{H}/N, regardless of nAn\_{A}.

If an AI scales by uniformly sampling more cues from a fixed pool, its overlap with a given human equals the human’s coverage fraction nH/Nn\_{H}/N in expectation (the share of all cues the human accesses), regardless of the AI’s capability. Overlap is therefore not tunable through AI scale alone. The invariance is a statement in expectation under uniform random sampling of 𝒳A\mathcal{X}\_{A}, not a claim that all AI systems in a domain share the same realized λ\lambda: two AI systems whose cue access is drawn from different sampling distributions (different training corpora, training objectives, or architectures) can yield different realized λ\lambda even within the same domain.

In the analysis that follows we consider (τH,τA,λ)(\tau\_{H},\tau\_{A},\lambda) as separate deployment parameters, because different humans paired with different AIs in different domains generate different parameter combinations. Two feasibility constraints on (τH,τA,λ)(\tau\_{H},\tau\_{A},\lambda) deserve note. The model-agnostic constraint, from positive semidefiniteness of the covariance matrix in Lemma [2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma1 "Lemma 2.1 (Joint distribution of log-likelihood ratios). ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), is τA≤τH/λ2\tau\_{A}\leq\tau\_{H}/\lambda^{2}. The cue-pool generative model imposes the tighter bound τA≤τH/λ\tau\_{A}\leq\tau\_{H}/\lambda (since n∩≤nHn\_{\cap}\leq n\_{H}); at this boundary, the AI’s evidence is Blackwell-equivalent to the human-AI team’s. All quantitative results in our analysis live within the cue-pool feasible region (which is contained in the broader PSD region).

After processing its cues, the AI communicates a sufficient statistic for ℓA\ell\_{A} to the human, such as a recommended answer, a probability report, or a textual explanation. We assume this communication is informationally equivalent to ℓA\ell\_{A} (the below analysis is agnostic to the format of the information). We refer to the human decision-maker who has communicated with AI and has access to (ℓH,ℓA)(\ell\_{H},\ell\_{A}) as the *worker*. The worker forms a posterior probability for Y=1Y=1 and provides a binary decision. We model the worker via two parameters that capture distinct primitives: one a belief about the joint distribution of signals, the other a behavioral discount on the AI’s contribution.

* • Correlation awareness α^∈[0,1]\hat{\alpha}\in[0,1] (a belief). The worker’s perceived overlap is α^⋅λ\hat{\alpha}\cdot\lambda. At α^=1\hat{\alpha}=1 she perceives overlap correctly; at α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0 she perceives the signals as conditionally independent (correlation neglect); intermediate values represent partial awareness. * • AI trust β^>0\hat{\beta}>0 (a behavioral discount). The worker applies a multiplicative weight β^\hat{\beta} to the AI signal ℓA\ell\_{A} in her decision statistic. At β^=1\hat{\beta}=1 she applies no behavioral discount; β^<1\hat{\beta}<1 corresponds to AI undertrust; β^>1\hat{\beta}>1 corresponds to overtrust.

Correlation awareness α^∈[0,1]\hat{\alpha}\in[0,1] (a belief). The worker’s perceived overlap is α^⋅λ\hat{\alpha}\cdot\lambda. At α^=1\hat{\alpha}=1 she perceives overlap correctly; at α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0 she perceives the signals as conditionally independent (correlation neglect); intermediate values represent partial awareness.

AI trust β^>0\hat{\beta}>0 (a behavioral discount). The worker applies a multiplicative weight β^\hat{\beta} to the AI signal ℓA\ell\_{A} in her decision statistic. At β^=1\hat{\beta}=1 she applies no behavioral discount; β^<1\hat{\beta}<1 corresponds to AI undertrust; β^>1\hat{\beta}>1 corresponds to overtrust.

These parameters are jointly identified from cross-AI variation in λ\lambda (Appendix [H](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A8 "Appendix H Identification of the worker’s parameters and regime tests ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")).
The worker has parameters (α^,β^)∈[0,1]×ℝ>0(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta})\in[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}\_{>0} and behaves as follows:

1. (i) *Bayesian updating under perceived overlap.* The worker performs Bayesian updating on (ℓH,ℓA,Y)(\ell\_{H},\ell\_{A},Y) under a belief that perceives overlap as α^​λ\hat{\alpha}\lambda and capabilities (τH,τA)(\tau\_{H},\tau\_{A}) at their true values. This produces a Bayesian posterior log-odds. 2. (ii) *Behavioral trust discount.* After Bayesian updating, the worker scales the AI signal lAl\_{A} by a multiplicative factor β^\hat{\beta} in the posterior log-odds. This discount is applied to the AI signal *after* Bayesian updating, with no underlying belief interpretation.

*Bayesian updating under perceived overlap.* The worker performs Bayesian updating on (ℓH,ℓA,Y)(\ell\_{H},\ell\_{A},Y) under a belief that perceives overlap as α^​λ\hat{\alpha}\lambda and capabilities (τH,τA)(\tau\_{H},\tau\_{A}) at their true values. This produces a Bayesian posterior log-odds.

Under this assumption and the Gaussian signal structure, the worker’s decision rule satisfies the following linear aggregation of the agent log-likelihood ratios. 33 3 Our linear behavioral rule, characterized by two behavioral parameters, is a substantial simplification adopted for conceptual clarity. Human and LLM reasoning in real-world settings may be considerably more complex, and we leave modeling this complexity to future work.

children.heading: Remark 2.5 (Why β^\hat{\beta} is a behavioral discount, not a belief).

content.text: A natural alternative interprets trust discount as a subjective belief about AI capability, replacing τA\tau\_{A} by β^​τA\hat{\beta}\tau\_{A} in the worker’s perceived signal distribution. Because any such subjective-capability model leaves the Bayesian weight on ℓA\ell\_{A} unchanged, rendering trust unidentifiable, we model β^\hat{\beta} as a behavioral discount applied after Bayesian updating; see Appendix [A](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A1 "Appendix A Behavioral modeling of trust miscalibration ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust").

The two-parameter family (α^,β^)∈[0,1]×ℝ>0(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta})\in[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}\_{>0} contains a continuum of worker behaviors. We consider two benchmarks at the extremes of correlation awareness.

Bayes-rational (BR). α^=1\hat{\alpha}=1, β^=1\hat{\beta}=1. The worker perceives overlap correctly and applies no trust discount. Substituting into Lemma [2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma4 "Lemma 2.4 (Worker’s decision weights). ‣ 2.1 The Worker’s Decision Rule ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") gives weights wHBR=τH−τA​λτH−τA​λ2w\_{H}^{\mathrm{BR}}=\frac{\tau\_{H}-\tau\_{A}\lambda}{\tau\_{H}-\tau\_{A}\lambda^{2}} and wABR=τH​(1−λ)τH−τA​λ2w\_{A}^{\mathrm{BR}}=\frac{\tau\_{H}(1-\lambda)}{\tau\_{H}-\tau\_{A}\lambda^{2}}. In the symmetric case τH=τA\tau\_{H}=\tau\_{A}, both weights equal 1/(1+λ)1/(1+\lambda), with the Bayesian shrinkage correcting for redundant evidence on both sides.

Correlation neglect (CN). α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0, β^\hat{\beta} arbitrary. The worker treats (ℓH,ℓA)(\ell\_{H},\ell\_{A}) as conditionally independent given YY, yielding ℓ^=ℓH+β^​ℓA\hat{\ell}=\ell\_{H}+\hat{\beta}\,\ell\_{A}. The case β^=1\hat{\beta}=1 is the classical CN agent; β^<1\hat{\beta}<1 also discounts the AI signal.

The benchmarks differ in how the AI weight responds to true overlap: wABRw\_{A}^{\mathrm{BR}} depends on λ\lambda, whereas wACN=β^w\_{A}^{\mathrm{CN}}=\hat{\beta} is invariant to λ\lambda — the CN worker treats AI evidence the same regardless of true redundancy. The interior of (α^,β^)(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}) space combines partial correlation awareness and trust miscalibration.

This section develops three results that guide the empirical study presented later. The first is a closed-form expression for the worker’s classification accuracy that, under correlation neglect (α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0), partitions the deployment space (τA,λ)(\tau\_{A},\lambda) into three regimes: *complementarity* (human-AI team is most accurate), *impairment* (human alone is most accurate), and *automation* (AI alone is most accurate). The second is a welfare decomposition: the worker’s loss against the Bayes-rational benchmark splits additively into a correlation-neglect cost and an undertrust cost, which could then be calculated by the identified behavioral parameters α^\hat{\alpha} and β^\hat{\beta}. Our results depend only on the joint-Gaussian structure of Lemma [2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma1 "Lemma 2.1 (Joint distribution of log-likelihood ratios). ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"); the cue-pool model is one interpretable construction yielding it, not a requirement.

The worker’s decision rule under Assumption [2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma3 "Assumption 2.3 (Worker’s behavior). ‣ 2.1 The Worker’s Decision Rule ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") can be evaluated using different performance objectives. We focus on binary-decision accuracy in the main text, which is the natural welfare statistic when the worker’s output is a binary label. Formally, the *accuracy* is the probability that the worker’s binary decision is correct: 𝒜:=P⁡(Y^=Y)\mathcal{A}:=P(\hat{Y}=Y), where Y^=𝟏{ℓ^>0}\hat{Y}=\mathbf{1}\{\hat{\ell}>0\} is her hardmax decision. Other objectives like log loss and switching-rate are derived and discussed in Appendix [B](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A2 "Appendix B More performance objectives ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") and are useful for probability reports and revision data.

Accuracy via the signal-to-noise (SNR) ratio. Under Assumption [2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma3 "Assumption 2.3 (Worker’s behavior). ‣ 2.1 The Worker’s Decision Rule ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), the worker’s decision statistic ℓ^=wH​ℓH+wA​ℓA\hat{\ell}=w\_{H}\ell\_{H}+w\_{A}\ell\_{A} is a linear combination of the jointly Gaussian pair (ℓH,ℓA)(\ell\_{H},\ell\_{A}) from Lemma [2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma1 "Lemma 2.1 (Joint distribution of log-likelihood ratios). ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"); hence ℓ^|Y\hat{\ell}\mid Y is itself Gaussian. Accuracy under the rule 𝟏{ℓ^>0}\mathbf{1}\{\hat{\ell}>0\} is a function of the SNR ratio of ℓ^\hat{\ell}, namely the ratio of the conditional mean’s magnitude to the conditional standard deviation.

The signal-to-noise ratio rH​Ar\_{HA} has a clear reading. Conditional on YY, the worker’s decision statistic ℓ^\hat{\ell} has mean (2​Y−1)​(wH​τH+wA​τA)(2Y-1)(w\_{H}\tau\_{H}+w\_{A}\tau\_{A}) and variance 2​(wH2​τH+wA2​τA+2​wH​wA​τA​λ)2(w\_{H}^{2}\tau\_{H}+w\_{A}^{2}\tau\_{A}+2w\_{H}w\_{A}\tau\_{A}\lambda). Bayes-rational rule is welfare-optimal. By Lemma [2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma1 "Lemma 2.1 (Joint distribution of log-likelihood ratios). ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), (ℓH,ℓA)|Y(\ell\_{H},\ell\_{A})\mid Y is Gaussian with shared covariance across YY; the linear direction maximizing rH​Ar\_{HA} from Lemma [3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.Thmlemma1 "Lemma 3.1 (Accuracy of the worker’s decision rule). ‣ 3.1 Performance Objective ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") therefore coincides with the Bayes-rational rule from §[2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.SS2 "2.2 Two Benchmarks ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), giving maximum SNR r∗:=rH​A​(α^=1,β^=1)r^{\*}:=r\_{HA}(\hat{\alpha}=1,\hat{\beta}=1) and optimal accuracy 𝒜BR=Φ⁡(r∗)\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{BR}}=\Phi(r^{\*}). The accuracy gap 𝒜BR−𝒜H​A​(α^,β^)≥0\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{BR}}-\mathcal{A}\_{HA}(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta})\geq 0 is the worker’s loss relative to the BR benchmark.

Comparing the three accuracies 𝒜H=Φ⁡(τH/2)\mathcal{A}\_{H}=\Phi(\sqrt{\tau\_{H}/2}), 𝒜H​A\mathcal{A}\_{HA} from Lemma [3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.Thmlemma1 "Lemma 3.1 (Accuracy of the worker’s decision rule). ‣ 3.1 Performance Objective ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), and 𝒜A​I=Φ⁡(τA/2)\mathcal{A}\_{AI}=\Phi(\sqrt{\tau\_{A}/2}) partitions the deployment space (τA,λ)(\tau\_{A},\lambda), for each fixed β^>0\hat{\beta}>0, into three regions: *complementarity* (HA optimal, i.e., the human-AI team is most accurate), *impairment* (H optimal), and *automation* (AI optimal). For clarity, we state the closed-form phase diagram at strict correlation neglect (α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0); the same qualitative forces extend continuously to partial correlation awareness, with larger α^\hat{\alpha} attenuating double-counting.

with τauto​(0,β^)=+∞\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(0;\hat{\beta})=+\infty if β^≥1/2\hat{\beta}\geq 1/2 and τH/(1−2​β^)\tau\_{H}/(1-2\hat{\beta}) otherwise. Then for τA>0\tau\_{A}>0:

* • *Low overlap* (λ≤1−β^/2\lambda\leq 1-\hat{\beta}/2, when β^<2\hat{\beta}<2): complementarity if τA<τauto​(λ,β^)\tau\_{A}<\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}); automation if τA≥τauto​(λ,β^)\tau\_{A}\geq\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}). * • *Moderate overlap* (1−β^/2<λ<11-\hat{\beta}/2<\lambda<1): impairment if τA<τaug​(λ,β^)\tau\_{A}<\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}); complementarity if τaug​(λ,β^)≤τA≤τauto​(λ,β^)\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta})\leq\tau\_{A}\leq\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}); automation if τA>τauto​(λ,β^)\tau\_{A}>\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}). * • *High overlap* (λ=1\lambda=1): the two thresholds coincide, τaug​(1,β^)=τauto​(1,β^)=τH\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}(1;\hat{\beta})=\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(1;\hat{\beta})=\tau\_{H}, so the complementarity region collapses to the single point τA=τH\tau\_{A}=\tau\_{H}.

*Low overlap* (λ≤1−β^/2\lambda\leq 1-\hat{\beta}/2, when β^<2\hat{\beta}<2): complementarity if τA<τauto​(λ,β^)\tau\_{A}<\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}); automation if τA≥τauto​(λ,β^)\tau\_{A}\geq\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}).

*Moderate overlap* (1−β^/2<λ<11-\hat{\beta}/2<\lambda<1): impairment if τA<τaug​(λ,β^)\tau\_{A}<\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}); complementarity if τaug​(λ,β^)≤τA≤τauto​(λ,β^)\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta})\leq\tau\_{A}\leq\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}); automation if τA>τauto​(λ,β^)\tau\_{A}>\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}).

*High overlap* (λ=1\lambda=1): the two thresholds coincide, τaug​(1,β^)=τauto​(1,β^)=τH\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}(1;\hat{\beta})=\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(1;\hat{\beta})=\tau\_{H}, so the complementarity region collapses to the single point τA=τH\tau\_{A}=\tau\_{H}.
Here, τaug\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}} is strictly increasing in λ\lambda on (1−β^/2,1](1-\hat{\beta}/2,1] and τauto\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}} is strictly decreasing in λ\lambda on (0,1](0,1].
The theorem yields several substantive insights that we elaborate below.

Insight 1: (Impairment Region) – A weak AI can hurt a worker who neglects correlation. The phase diagram has an *impairment* region where the worker assisted by the AI does worse than the worker alone (𝒜H​A<𝒜H\mathcal{A}\_{HA}<\mathcal{A}\_{H}). From Theorem [3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.Thmlemma2 "Theorem 3.2 (Phase diagram under correlation neglect). ‣ 3.2 Phase Diagram ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), this region exists whenever overlap satisfies λ>1−β^/2\lambda>1-\hat{\beta}/2. The mechanism is direct. When overlap is high, much of the AI’s evidence is content the worker already has. The correlation-neglect worker, using the rule ℓ^=ℓH+β^​ℓA\hat{\ell}=\ell\_{H}+\hat{\beta}\ell\_{A}, treats ℓA\ell\_{A} as if it were a fresh, independent signal. By giving ℓA\ell\_{A} full weight β^\hat{\beta}, she effectively double-counts the overlapping content. When the AI is weak (small τA\tau\_{A}), the genuinely new information in ℓA\ell\_{A} is too small to offset the double-counting penalty, and her accuracy falls below the human-alone benchmark.

Insight 2: (Automation Region) – Automation is inevitable as AI capability grows. From Theorem [3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.Thmlemma2 "Theorem 3.2 (Phase diagram under correlation neglect). ‣ 3.2 Phase Diagram ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), the automation threshold τauto​(λ,β^)\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}) is finite for any λ>0\lambda>0, so AI alone outperforms the team whenever τA>τauto\tau\_{A}>\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}. The cue-pool interpretation imposes an upper bound τA≤τH/λ\tau\_{A}\leq\tau\_{H}/\lambda; at this boundary the AI’s evidence is Blackwell-equivalent to the team’s, so automation is welfare-optimal regardless of trust calibration. Since τauto​(λ,β^)<τH/λ\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta})<\tau\_{H}/\lambda for all λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), automation is reached at finite AI capability strictly inside the feasible region. This contrasts with the Bayes-rational case, where the team weakly outperforms either modality and strict automation is never optimal; therefore, under correlation neglect, inevitable automation is a signature of behavioral misspecification, not of the underlying information structure.

Insight 3: (Complementarity Region) – The complementarity region narrows as overlap grows. For any fixed β^>0\hat{\beta}>0, the complementarity region in the (τA,λ)(\tau\_{A},\lambda) plane has the form τA∈[τaug​(λ,β^),τauto​(λ,β^)]\tau\_{A}\in[\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}),\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta})] when both thresholds are positive. As λ\lambda rises: the augmentation threshold τaug\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}} is strictly increasing: more overlap requires a more capable AI before the team beats the human alone; meanwhile, the automation threshold τauto\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}} is strictly decreasing: more overlap means a less capable AI suffices for AI alone to beat the team. Therefore, the complementarity region shrinks from both ends as λ\lambda grows, and at λ=1\lambda=1 collapses to the single tie point τA=τH\tau\_{A}=\tau\_{H}.

Insight 4: Trust is a double-edged lever under correlation neglect. The worker’s trust β^\hat{\beta} scales how strongly she weights the AI signal, with opposing effects across the two phase boundaries.

children.heading: Corollary 3.3 (Comparative statics of phase boundaries in trust).

content.text: The phase boundaries are strictly increasing in β^\hat{\beta} for λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1): ∂τaug∂β^>0\frac{\partial\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}}{\partial\hat{\beta}}>0 and ∂τauto∂β^>0\frac{\partial\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}}{\partial\hat{\beta}}>0.

A worker who trusts the AI signal more benefits more from its marginal information but also incurs a larger double-counting penalty. This has opposite effects at the two boundaries. At the lower boundary, higher trust amplifies double-counting when the AI is weak and redundant, so a more capable AI is needed before assistance beats the human-alone benchmark. Similarly, higher trust will also make the lowest level of overlap needed for impairment, 1−β^/21-\hat{\beta}/2, lower. At the upper boundary, higher trust also lets the human-AI team make better use of a strong AI signal, so AI-alone dominance is delayed. Thus undertrust is protective against harmful redundant AI but makes automation arrive sooner, while overtrust expands impairment but can preserve complementarity up to higher AI capability.

Accuracy as a function of AI capability. Figure [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Phase Diagram ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") traces 𝒜H\mathcal{A}\_{H}, 𝒜H​A\mathcal{A}\_{HA}, 𝒜A​I\mathcal{A}\_{AI} vs. τA\tau\_{A} at three overlap levels while fixing β^=1\hat{\beta}=1, τH=1\tau\_{H}=1. At low overlap, 𝒜H​A\mathcal{A}\_{HA} rises monotonically and dominates 𝒜H\mathcal{A}\_{H} until 𝒜A​I\mathcal{A}\_{AI} overtakes it at τauto\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}. At moderate overlap, 𝒜H​A\mathcal{A}\_{HA} is non-monotone: it dips below 𝒜H\mathcal{A}\_{H} for small τA\tau\_{A} (impairment), crosses at τaug\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}, and is overtaken by 𝒜A​I\mathcal{A}\_{AI} at τauto\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}. At λ=1\lambda=1, the complementarity interval collapses to the triple tie at τA=τH\tau\_{A}=\tau\_{H}. The non-monotonicity is the signature of correlation neglect: weak AI hurts via double-counting, moderate AI helps once its marginal information dominates, strong AI eventually dominates as the worker becomes a noise channel.

The design implications are threefold. First, AI systems serving correlation-neglect workers benefit from *reducing* effective overlap with human evidence, not just from increasing τA\tau\_{A}: at fixed τA\tau\_{A} the team SNR is strictly decreasing in λ\lambda (∂rH​A2/∂λ|α^=0<0\partial r\_{HA}^{2}/\partial\lambda|\_{\hat{\alpha}=0}<0 for any β^>0\hat{\beta}>0), giving the principle of training AI to predict what humans miss rather than what they already know. Second, whether to provide ℓA\ell\_{A} at all is a complementary lever: from Theorem [3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.Thmlemma2 "Theorem 3.2 (Phase diagram under correlation neglect). ‣ 3.2 Phase Diagram ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), the team is welfare-optimal only on τA∈[τaug​(λ,β^),τauto​(λ,β^)]\tau\_{A}\in[\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta}),\,\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}(\lambda;\hat{\beta})], so the optimal disclosure rule is to withhold ℓA\ell\_{A} when τA<τaug\tau\_{A}<\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}}, provide it when τA∈[τaug,τauto]\tau\_{A}\in[\tau\_{\mathrm{aug}},\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}], and automate when τA>τauto\tau\_{A}>\tau\_{\mathrm{auto}}. Third, in the impairment region, behavioral interventions encouraging *undertrust* (β^<1\hat{\beta}<1) can improve welfare for correlation-neglect workers: β^<1\hat{\beta}<1 does not correct the neglect but dampens its double-counting cost (Corollary [3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.Thmlemma3 "Corollary 3.3 (Comparative statics of phase boundaries in trust). ‣ 3.2 Phase Diagram ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")), so the conventional calibration target β^=1\hat{\beta}=1 is not welfare-optimal there.

The phase diagram characterizes which deployment mode yields the highest accuracy. We now consider a complementary question: how much accuracy does the worker lose relative to the Bayes-rational benchmark, and how much of this loss is attributable to correlation neglect versus undertrust?

Write 𝒜⁡(α^,β^)\mathcal{A}(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}) for the worker’s accuracy under behavioral primitives α^\hat{\alpha} and β\beta, and let 𝒜BR=𝒜⁡(1,1)\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{BR}}=\mathcal{A}(1,1) be the Bayesian rational benchmark. We define

Here, TWL\mathrm{TWL} is the worker’s total welfare loss compared to the BR benchmark, which subsequently decomposes into two types of loss, CNC\mathrm{CNC} and UTC\mathrm{UTC}. The correlation-neglect cost CNC\mathrm{CNC} measures the loss from imperfect correlation awareness when trust is calibrated. The undertrust cost UTC\mathrm{UTC} measures the gain from calibrating trust while holding the worker’s actual awareness level fixed. We have the following exact decomposition.

Within the cue-pool feasible region, for every worker (α^,β^)∈[0,1]×ℝ>0(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta})\in[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}\_{>0}, we have TWL⁡(α^,β^)=CNC⁡(α^)+UTC⁡(α^,β^)\mathrm{TWL}(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta})=\mathrm{CNC}(\hat{\alpha})+\mathrm{UTC}(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}). The correlation-neglect component is nonnegative: CNC⁡(α^)≥0\mathrm{CNC}(\hat{\alpha})\geq 0. If β^∈(0,1]\hat{\beta}\in(0,1] and τA≥τH\tau\_{A}\geq\tau\_{H}, the undertrust component is also nonnegative; it vanishes when β^=1\hat{\beta}=1.

As mentioned before, the two types of loss correspond to two design levers. Calibrating trust first recovers UTC\mathrm{UTC}; correcting the remaining correlation misperception then recovers CNC\mathrm{CNC}. We will later link this welfare decomposition to our empirical study. Finally, we define the welfare gain relative to the unaided human,
It is used to measure the benefit of AI assistance relative to human-alone performance. It is also used in our empirical study.

We instantiate the framework on ChatBench ([Chang et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib6)), a controlled MTurk study in which 643643 workers answer multiple-choice questions from MMLU ([Hendrycks et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib5)) across math, physics, and moral reasoning. Each worker is randomly assigned to one of two AI assistants (GPT-4o or Llama-3.1-8b) under an answer-first protocol: she records an unassisted answer with stated confidence, then sees the AI’s response and records a final answer. After matching the answer-first user-AI rows to their corresponding user-alone rows and restricting to pairs where the AI committed to a definite letter recommendation, we obtain 2,1992{,}199 paired observations covering 315315 workers and 389389 questions. We construct ℓH=logit⁡(pH​(c))\ell\_{H}=\mathrm{logit}(p\_{H}(c)) from worker confidence and ℓAm,q=logit⁡(pAm,q)\ell\_{A}^{m,q}=\mathrm{logit}(p\_{A}^{m,q}) from AI model mm’s empirical accuracy on question qq across up to 5050 generations. The binary outcome YY is the ground-truth letter. Appendix [G](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A7 "Appendix G Sample construction ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") details sample construction.

AI assistant produces significant welfare gains; different AI models lead to different optimal deployment modes Workers go from 𝒜H=0.612\mathcal{A}\_{H}=0.612 alone to 𝒜H​A=0.824\mathcal{A}\_{HA}=0.824 with AI assistance, a pooled welfare gain of GAP=+0.213\mathrm{GAP}=+0.213 (95% CI [0.191,0.235][0.191,0.235], never negative in 1,0001{,}000 bootstrap samples). The two deployments fall in different empirical regimes (Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")). For GPT-4o, the AI alone outperforms the team (𝒜A​I=0.884>𝒜H​A=0.851\mathcal{A}\_{AI}=0.884>\mathcal{A}\_{HA}=0.851, p=0.002p=0.002): GPT is firmly in the framework’s *automation* regime. For Llama-3.1-8b, 𝒜H​A=0.795\mathcal{A}\_{HA}=0.795 and 𝒜A​I=0.787\mathcal{A}\_{AI}=0.787 are statistically indistinguishable (p=0.55p=0.55), placing Llama at the *boundary* between complementarity and automation. The cross-deployment GAP gap of +0.081+0.081 is approximately 93%93\% explained by capability composition (95% CI [68%,148%][68\%,148\%]); a likelihood-ratio test of cell-by-AI interactions gives χ2​(4)=0.96\chi^{2}(4)=0.96, p=0.92p=0.92. This validates the framework’s central qualitative claim that AI capability τAm\tau\_{A}^{m} governs deployment-level welfare while behavior is approximately invariant across deployments.

Workers substantially undertrust the AI; strict correlation neglect is rejected. Inverting Lemma [2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma4 "Lemma 2.4 (Worker’s decision weights). ‣ 2.1 The Worker’s Decision Rule ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") from per-deployment logistic regression weights identifies β^=0.285\hat{\beta}=0.285 (95% CI [0.246,0.322][0.246,0.322]): workers apply roughly a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to the AI signal. A second approach using cross-question variation to estimate λ\lambda directly gives β^=0.254\hat{\beta}=0.254, in close agreement; see Appendix [H](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A8 "Appendix H Identification of the worker’s parameters and regime tests ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"). Both decisively reject β^=1\hat{\beta}=1. Strict correlation neglect (α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0) is also rejected: the inversion’s residual sum of squares jumps 141141-fold when α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0 is forced, and direct λ^\hat{\lambda} is positive in 100%100\% of bootstrap samples for both deployments. The data does not pin down α^\hat{\alpha} to a narrow range but decisively rejects this corner case.

Overlap λ\lambda varies meaningfully across AIs and across subject domains. Direct λ\lambda estimation from cross-question variation gives two empirical patterns that connect back to the framework’s cue-pool picture of overlap (Proposition [2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma2 "Proposition 2.2 (Overlap as a domain property). ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")). First, λ\lambda differs significantly across the two AIs: λ^Llama=0.127\hat{\lambda}^{\text{Llama}}=0.127 exceeds λ^GPT=0.071\hat{\lambda}^{\text{GPT}}=0.071 by +0.056+0.056 (95% CI [0.015,0.097][0.015,0.097], two-sided p≈0.009p\approx 0.009). The smaller model’s evidence overlaps more with what humans access; GPT brings more genuinely novel information. Second, λ\lambda varies dramatically across subjects, pooled across both AIs: math λ^≈0.20\hat{\lambda}\approx 0.20, physics λ^≈0.04\hat{\lambda}\approx 0.04, moral reasoning λ^≈0\hat{\lambda}\approx 0, with the same pattern holding within each AI separately. Domains where humans and AI rely on shared informational cues exhibit substantial overlap; domains where reasoning paths are more idiosyncratic exhibit essentially none. Proposition [2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma2 "Proposition 2.2 (Overlap as a domain property). ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") characterizes overlap as a property of the human-domain pair under uniform cue sampling; the cross-AI heterogeneity indicates that real AIs’ training data is more complicated.

Trust calibration and design implications. Section [3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.SS3 "3.3 Welfare Decomposition ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") splits the worker’s accuracy loss against the Bayes-rational benchmark into a correlation-neglect cost CNC\mathrm{CNC} and an undertrust cost UTC\mathrm{UTC}, with UTC\mathrm{UTC} the accuracy recovered by calibrating trust (Proposition [3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.Thmlemma4 "Proposition 3.4 (Welfare decomposition). ‣ 3.3 Welfare Decomposition ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")). Here, we measure the empirical counterpart of UTC\mathrm{UTC}. On items where the worker’s unaided answer and the AI’s recommendation disagree, we replace her final choice with a simulated trust-calibrated rule that selects whichever answer is more likely correct given the same two signals used to identify the behavioral parameters, her stated confidence ℓH\ell\_{H} and the AI’s question-level accuracy ℓA\ell\_{A}. Here, the correctness probabilities are estimated by cross-validated logistic regression (Appendix [K](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A11 "Appendix K Empirical welfare evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")). Like UTC\mathrm{UTC}, the resulting gain isolates the trust channel: it changes how she relies on the AI. For GPT-4o, the simulated rule follows the AI on about 92%92\% of disagreements, versus the real workers’ 70%70\%, and raises team accuracy by 2.62.6 percentage points, from 0.8510.851 to 0.8770.877, close to the AI-alone accuracy of 0.8840.884. So for GPT-4o, which lies in the automation regime, calibrating trust moves the team nearly to the AI-alone benchmark. For Llama-3.1-8b, which sits at the complementarity-automation boundary, the simulated rule instead does worse than the actual workers (−1.4-1.4 percentage points). The reason is informational rather than behavioral: the simulated rule sees only two coarse signals, whereas the worker also reads the AI’s specific answer and can judge its reasoning, which for the weaker AI evidently outweighs calibrating trust. Two design implications follow from the result. First, trust calibration pays off more where the AI is strong, so interventions that raise trust should be targeted to AI-strong cases rather than applied uniformly. Meanwhile, besides behavior calibration, the granularity of information the worker receives is equally important.

Extensions to other applications. The contribution of our empirical framework extends beyond ChatBench’s setup with MMLU questions, and can be applied to other domains such as medicine, law, or programming, where human and AI expertise are combined. Estimating the model’s primitives requires only the observables present in any binary classification setting: the human-alone report ℓH\ell\_{H}, the AI-alone report ℓA\ell\_{A}, the AI-assisted human’s report ℓ^\hat{\ell}, and the ground-truth label YY. An example is professional radiologists diagnosing from X-ray imagery with and without AI assistance as in [Agarwal et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib12): ground truth comes from an expert diagnostic panel, the human and AI signals are the prior-corrected logits of the human-alone and AI-alone probability reports, and the same class-conditional moments identify τH,τA,λ,α^\tau\_{H},\tau\_{A},\lambda,\hat{\alpha}, and β^\hat{\beta}.

Broader impacts. Our framework characterizes when sharing an AI recommendation helps or harms a human decision-maker, and identifies two levers for improving deployed human-AI teams: calibrating trust and reducing information overlap. Positively, the phase diagram offers deployment guidance (withhold, assist, or automate) that can prevent the accuracy losses documented when capable AI is naively added to human workflows, and the overlap lever suggests training assistants to supply complementary rather than redundant evidence. Risks include over-reliance on a stylized two-signal model: the behavioral parameters are estimated from a specific crowdsourced setting (ChatBench/MMLU) and need not transfer to high-stakes domains such as medicine or hiring, where miscalibrated ‘automation’ recommendations could cause harm. Our prescriptions should be treated as a modeling-informed starting point for extensive domain-specific validation.

We build a model of AI-assisted classification in which a worker combines her own evidence with an AI’s through two behavioral primitives, correlation awareness and trust. We derive a closed-form phase diagram over capability and overlap that separates complementarity, impairment, and automation. We examine the framework on ChatBench, finding substantial undertrust, regimes decided by AI capability and overlap, and heterogeneous gains from trust calibration. The framework potentially applies to any setup of AI-assisted decision making where human-alone, AI-alone, AI-assisted assessment, and ground truth are all observed.

content.text: A natural alternative to model trust miscalibration is to interpret trust as a subjective belief about the AI’s capability, replacing τA\tau\_{A} by β^​τA\hat{\beta}\tau\_{A} in the worker’s perceived signal distribution. This interpretation is not appropriate for the present classification model. The AI’s message is assumed to be informationally equivalent to its log-likelihood ratio ℓA\ell\_{A}, or equivalently to a calibrated posterior probability. Once ℓA\ell\_{A} is observed, its Bayesian contribution to posterior log-odds is already encoded in its realized value.

Thus, changing the worker’s perceived AI precision changes the ex ante distribution she assigns to ℓA\ell\_{A}, but it does not change the Bayesian weight placed on ℓA\ell\_{A} as long as the worker still believes expit⁡(ℓA)\expit(\ell\_{A}) is a calibrated forecast. In particular, under perceived independence, any subjective-capability model yields the decision statistic ℓ^=ℓH+ℓA\hat{\ell}=\ell\_{H}+\ell\_{A}, so trust would be behaviorally unidentifiable.

For this reason, we model β^\hat{\beta} as a behavioral weight on the AI’s communicated likelihood-ratio contribution, rather than as a subjective precision. β^≠1\hat{\beta}\neq 1 should be interpreted as a departure from treating the AI’s probability report as a fully trusted calibrated posterior. If β^<1\hat{\beta}<1, the worker behaves as though the AI’s log-odds are too extreme and shrinks them toward zero; if β^>1\hat{\beta}>1, she behaves as though the AI’s log-odds are too conservative and amplifies them.

The *expected log loss* is ℒlog:=𝔼⁡[−log⁡P⁡(Y∣ℓ^)]\mathcal{L}\_{\log}:=\mathbb{E}[-\log P(Y\mid\hat{\ell})], where P⁡(Y∣ℓ^)=expit⁡((2​Y−1)​ℓ^)P(Y\mid\hat{\ell})=\expit((2Y-1)\hat{\ell}) is the worker’s reported probability for the realized state. The log loss is the natural statistic when the worker’s output is a probability rather than a binary decision. Unlike the error rate, which only depends on whether the decision is correct, log loss also penalizes the confidence with which the worker reports a wrong answer.

The log loss differs from the error rate in a substantive way. The error rate scores only whether the binary decision Y^=𝟏{ℓ^>0}\hat{Y}=\mathbf{1}\{\hat{\ell}>0\} is correct; it ignores the magnitude |ℓ^||\hat{\ell}|. The log loss scores both the direction of the worker’s belief and her confidence in it. Two workers with the same correctness rate can have different log losses if their probability reports differ in how confidently wrong they are: a worker who reports p^=0.99\hat{p}=0.99 on an answer that turns out wrong pays more under log loss than a worker who reports p^=0.6\hat{p}=0.6 on the same wrong answer. The log loss therefore captures *calibration* of probability reports, while the error rate captures only point-estimate correctness.

Log loss is the relevant welfare objective when the worker’s task involves communicating probabilities rather than binary decisions: medical diagnosis with uncertainty estimates or any setting where downstream users act on the worker’s confidence and not just her hard recommendation. In binary-decision settings, where the worker’s output is a hard label, error rate is the appropriate welfare objective.

We show that each SNR-ray has a unique *calibrated point* where σ2=2​m\sigma^{2}=2m, where the statistic is a true log-likelihood ratio and its accuracy equals that of a calibrated single agent with signal-to-noise ratio rr; moreover, accuracy along the SNR-ray is maximized at the calibrated point, which is the unique maximum iff π≠1/2\pi\neq 1/2. This yields a *two-step SNR-ray projection lemma* that upper bounds 𝒜⁡(m,σ)\mathcal{A}\left(m,\sigma\right) by a selected single agent’s accuracy: if the team is weakly dominated by a single agent at prior 1/21/2, its signal-to-noise ratio is at most that agent’s; thus, under any prior π\pi, the team performance 𝒜⁡(m,σ)\mathcal{A}\left(m,\sigma\right) is still at most the accuracy at the calibrated point 𝒜⁡(2​m2/σ2,2​m/σ)\mathcal{A}\left(2m^{2}/\sigma^{2},2m/\sigma\right) with the same signal-to-noise ratio, which is itself upper bounded by the single agent’s accuracy. The ChatBench public release [[Chang et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib6)] contains 5,8715{,}871 conversation logs (conversations.json), 10,45010{,}450 user-answer rows (user\_answers\_filtered.csv) covering 643643 workers, and 792792 per-question AI-accuracy records (ai\_alone\_answers.csv) summarizing up to 5050 free-text generations per AI-question pair (mean 49.949.9; 77 pairs have fewer due to sampling failures). We construct the matched answer-first sample as follows.

Restrict conversations.json to rows with condition = answer-first and answer\_type = user-AI (the answer-first user-AI rows). Restrict user\_answers\_filtered.csv to answer\_type = user-alone with non-missing confidence (the user-alone rows). Inner-join on (worker\_id, question\_id, model) to pair each post-AI answer with its unaided counterpart. Merge ai\_alone\_answers.csv on (model, question\_id) to attach the per-question AI accuracy free\_text\_acc. This produces 2,8942{,}894 matched pairs.

Each MMLU question has a unique correct letter. We recover ground truth from the user-alone sample by taking selected\_answer of any worker who got the question right unaided. For two of the 396396 questions in the matched sample, no user got the question right alone; we drop the resulting 1010 rows (0.3%0.3\% of 2,8942{,}894) so that the AI-correctness indicator is well-defined for every observation. The remaining sample size is 2,8842{,}884.

The conversation logs include a flag conv\_has\_answer indicating whether the AI committed to a definite letter recommendation in its message. Pairs with conv\_has\_answer = True form the *Has-Rec* sample (2,1992{,}199 rows; 315315 unique workers; 389389 unique questions); the rest form the No-Rec sample (685685 rows). All analyses in §[4](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S4 "4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") use the Has-Rec sample, where the AI’s signal is unambiguously a labeled recommendation.

The two parameters are separately identified if the same worker population is observed paired with two AI systems that differ in their overlap with the human’s evidence. Domains where humans and AI rely on shared procedural cues (math) exhibit substantial overlap; domains where reasoning paths are more idiosyncratic (moral reasoning) exhibit essentially none. This provides empirical content for the cue-pool framing: under the model, λ\lambda is a property of the human-domain pair (Proposition [2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2.Thmlemma2 "Proposition 2.2 (Overlap as a domain property). ‣ 2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")); the data shows the predicted variation across domains and additionally a cross-AI effect that the uniform-sampling model does not predict.

children.heading: Information and the limits of the benchmark.

content.text: In reality, the worker observes more than the two predictors available to the fitted rule. In particular, she reads the AI’s actual answer and can assess its reasoning and relevance to the question. The question-level accuracy measure averages across responses and omits these response-specific information. Workers’ superior performance relative to the fitted rule in the Llama deployment is consistent with their using this additional information.

The broader implication is that improving human–AI performance may require attention to information as well as behavior. Better-calibrated trust offers a measurable opportunity in the stronger-AI deployment, but a rule based only on coarse confidence and accuracy measures does not capture the worker’s full decision problem. Richer response-specific information would allow a more informative benchmark and a clearer assessment of the remaining scope for behavioral improvement.

children.heading: Appendix L Departures from theory and what they mean

content.text: The framework of §§[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2 "2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")–[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3 "3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") is a binary-classification model with a Gaussian generative process, symmetric prior, and linear-rule decision-maker. The empirical setting departs from each of these in ways the analysis must accommodate.

children.heading: Binary reduction of a four-way task.

content.text: ChatBench is a four-way multiple-choice task; the model is binary. We define the outcome YiY\_{i} as the indicator that the worker’s chosen letter matches the unique correct letter on item ii, collapsing the three wrong letters into Yi=0Y\_{i}=0. Two consequences follow. *(i)* The model’s closed-form AI accuracy Φ⁡(τ^Ad/2)\Phi(\sqrt{\hat{\tau}\_{A}^{d}/2}) does not match empirical accuracy: at τ^ALlama=1.64\hat{\tau}\_{A}^{\text{Llama}}=1.64 the formula gives 0.820.82 versus empirical 𝒜A​ILlama=0.787\mathcal{A}\_{AI}^{\text{Llama}}=0.787, and at τ^AGPT=2.02\hat{\tau}\_{A}^{\text{GPT}}=2.02 it gives 0.840.84 versus empirical 0.8840.884. We do not use the closed-form accuracy formula anywhere in the empirical section; every accuracy reported in §[4](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S4 "4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") and Tables [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") and [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A11.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Constructing the simulated policy. ‣ Appendix K Empirical welfare evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") is the empirical sample mean. *(ii)* The empirical base rate Pr^​(h​\_​a​c​c=1)=0.612\widehat{\Pr}(h\\_acc=1)=0.612 is not 0.50.5, so the symmetric-prior assumption underlying Φ⁡(τ^H/2)=Pr⁡(h​\_​a​c​c=1)\Phi(\sqrt{\hat{\tau}\_{H}/2})=\Pr(h\\_acc=1) does not literally hold. We use prior-free conditional-mean estimators for τ^H\hat{\tau}\_{H} and τ^Ad\hat{\tau}\_{A}^{d} (Appendix [H](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A8 "Appendix H Identification of the worker’s parameters and regime tests ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")), which are invariant to the base rate.

About 62%62\% of Has-Rec rows have pAm,q∈{0,1}p\_{A}^{m,q}\in\{0,1\} (Appendix [G](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A7 "Appendix G Sample construction ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")), saturating ℓA\ell\_{A} at ±5.293\pm 5.293. Saturation is more severe for GPT-4o, where pAm,q=1p\_{A}^{m,q}=1 on the majority of items, than for Llama-3.1-8b. As a consequence, per-deployment regression coefficients w^Ad\hat{w}\_{A}^{d} are not on the same scale across deployments: w^AGPT\hat{w}\_{A}^{\text{GPT}} effectively measures the response to a near-binary "AI is right" indicator, while w^ALlama\hat{w}\_{A}^{\text{Llama}} uses more variation. Approach 1 (§[H](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A8 "Appendix H Identification of the worker’s parameters and regime tests ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")) absorbs this scale difference through the structural inversion, which divides through τ^Ad\hat{\tau}\_{A}^{d} when recovering β^\hat{\beta}. Approach 2 uses cross-question covariance and is invariant to monotone rescaling of ℓA\ell\_{A}. Direct comparison of w^Ad\hat{w}\_{A}^{d} across deployments would not be valid; the structural recovery of β^\hat{\beta} is.

The cue-pool model of §[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2 "2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") motivates λ\lambda as the fraction of the AI’s cues also accessed by the human. Language-model decisions are not literally generated by sampling discrete cues from a finite pool. We do not commit to the cue-pool generative process. The structural objects we estimate — the joint distribution of (ℓH,ℓA,Y)(\ell\_{H},\ell\_{A},Y) and its summary statistics (τH,τA,λ)(\tau\_{H},\tau\_{A},\lambda) — are well-defined regardless of the underlying generative process. The cue-pool story provides intuition for the cross-domain λ\lambda heterogeneity in Appendix [J](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A10 "Appendix J Overlap heterogeneity across AIs and subjects ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), but it is not required for the identification or welfare results.

ChatBench randomizes each worker to exactly one AI, so the GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-8b samples are disjoint worker pools. Cross-deployment comparisons therefore rely on random assignment rather than within-worker variation. Random assignment makes large population-level imbalances unlikely in expectation but does not rule out them in any specific sample. The behavioral-homogeneity test of Appendix [I](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A9 "Appendix I Capability-versus-behavior decomposition ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") (χ2​(4)=0.96\chi^{2}(4)=0.96, p=0.92p=0.92) provides a direct check: per-cell response rates are statistically indistinguishable across the two AI populations, supporting the cross-deployment comparability of β^\hat{\beta} and other behavioral parameters.

All empirical claims in Section [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S4 "4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") and Appendices [G](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A7 "Appendix G Sample construction ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")–[K](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A11 "Appendix K Empirical welfare evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") are computed by a single self-contained Python script that takes the three raw ChatBench files as input. It reproduces sample construction, signal calibration, the headline findings with bootstrap CIs (1,0001{,}000 direct, 200200 structural, 500500 welfare), all regime, correlation-neglect, capability-share, and λ\lambda-heterogeneity tests, the β^=1\hat{\beta}=1 counterfactual, and three robustness checks (worker-cluster bootstrap on all four headline quantities, ϵ\epsilon sensitivity, 55-fold cross-validated linear ceiling). All seeds are fixed; reference values appear in the script header; total runtime is approximately 44 minutes on a single CPU core. The script will be provided with the camera-ready version.

chunks.text: # AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust

heading_path: AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust
chunks.text:
###### Abstract

When does an AI assistant improve human decision-making, and when does it hurt? We argue that the answer depends not just on AI accuracy but also on how much its evidence overlaps with the human’s and how the human combines the two. A worker makes a binary decision by observing her own signal and receiving a recommendation from an AI. We develop a human behavioral model with two primitives: her awareness of the overlap and her trust in the AI. Our analysis gives a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability and overlap, with regions of complementarity, impairment, and automation. A worker who neglects the overlap (correlation neglect) can be made less accurate by a more capable AI, double-counting the shared evidence. Trust reshapes the regions - undertrust may compensate for correlation neglect, so that the trust level maximizing accuracy depends on the deployment parameters. Empirically, we identify the two model parameters by pairing the same workers with different AIs, and break the accuracy loss into a correlation-neglect cost and an undertrust cost, one tied to reducing overlap on the AI side, the other to calibrating trust on the human side. On ChatBench, AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 points, yet workers apply only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to AI information; GPT-4o falls in the automation region and Llama-3.1-8b stays at the complementarity boundary; and calibrating trust recovers about 2.6 points for GPT-4o but almost nothing for Llama-3.1-8b.

## 1 Introduction

Empirical evaluations of human-AI teams reach very different conclusions. Some studies report large accuracy gains from AI assistance ([Tschandl et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib11); [Steyvers et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib2)), while many find no improvement over the unaided human, or outright degradation: a more capable AI can hurt team performance ([Bansal et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib8)), AI explanations need not help ([Bansal et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib9)), AI predictions may not improve expert radiologists ([Agarwal et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib12)), and a meta-analysis across tasks and systems finds that human-AI teams on average perform worse ([Vaccaro et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib7)). We argue that whether assistance helps turns not on the AI’s accuracy alone, but also on how much its evidence overlaps the human’s and on how the human combines it with her own. For example, when a worker treats overlapping evidence as if it were independent, she counts the shared part twice, a bias documented as correlation neglect in belief formation ([Enke and Zimmermann, 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib4); [Eyster and Weizsacker, 2010](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib1)), and the team can end up less accurate than the worker alone. This paper constructs a model built on these factors, uses it to characterize when AI assistance helps and when it hurts, and develops an empirical estimation strategy that exploits variation of outputs obtained by pairing the same workers with different AIs.

We study a binary classification problem in which the human and the AI each hold evidence about the state, summarized by their log-likelihood ratios ℓH\ell\_{H} and ℓA\ell\_{A}, and the worker decides by the sign of a weighted sum wH​ℓH+wA​ℓAw\_{H}\ell\_{H}+w\_{A}\ell\_{A}. The model has two parts. In the *observation model*, each agent’s evidence is a collection of *cues*, and the key primitive is the *overlap coefficient* λ\lambda, the share of the AI’s cues the human already holds. In the *behavioral model*, the worker combines the two signals through correlation awareness α^∈[0,1]\hat{\alpha}\in[0,1], representing how well she accounts for that overlap, and trust β^>0\hat{\beta}>0, how much weight she puts on the AI information. Two benchmarks sit inside this family. The *Bayes-rational* worker (α^=1,β^=1\hat{\alpha}=1,\hat{\beta}=1) de-correlates and weights optimally, while the *correlation-neglect* worker (α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0) treats the two signals as independent. Overlap is a property of the information, awareness and trust are properties of the worker, and together they determine the team’s accuracy.

Our first results compare team performance against human and AI alone. Under the Bayes-rational benchmark the team is at least as accurate as either source alone, and strictly more accurate unless the AI’s evidence already contains the human’s. The impairment and automation outcomes seen in the literature, outside that case, must then come from the worker’s behavior rather than from the information structure. Away from that benchmark, we obtain a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability τA\tau\_{A} and overlap λ\lambda with three regions, complementarity where the team is most accurate, impairment where the unaided human is, and automation where the AI alone is. Two of its features run against intuition. The first is that a more capable AI can make the team less accurate. When overlap is high (λ>1−β^/2\lambda>1-\hat{\beta}/2), a stronger AI only gives a correlation-neglecting worker more evidence to double-count, and that can lower accuracy. The second is that undertrust is not simply an error to be corrected. Reducing trust shrinks the impairment region but brings automation on at lower capability, so the trust level that maximizes team accuracy is not always β^=1\hat{\beta}=1 but depends on the deployment parameters.

Our second set of results turns the model into a measurement tool. A Bayes-rational worker’s weight on the AI changes with overlap, while a correlation-neglecting worker’s does not, and this difference lets us estimate the parameters by pairing the same workers with two AIs of different overlap. Trust β^\hat{\beta} is sharply identified, while awareness α^\hat{\alpha} is only weakly identified because the overlap coefficient in our experiment is relatively small. We then split the worker’s accuracy loss against the Bayes-rational benchmark into two parts that add up exactly at any level of awareness, a correlation-neglect cost from misperceiving the overlap and an undertrust cost from underweighting the AI. Each is tied to a distinct lever on opposite sides of the information-behavior divide: reducing overlap on the AI side by training it to supply what the human lacks, and calibrating trust on the human side.

We examine the framework in the context of ChatBench ([Chang et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib6)), where 643 workers answer multiple-choice questions paired with either GPT-4o or Llama-3.1-8b. AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 percentage points, yet workers put only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight on the AI (β^=0.285\hat{\beta}=0.285). GPT-4o is more capable and overlaps the human less, so it lies in the automation regime, where the AI alone beats the team; Llama-3.1-8b is weaker and overlaps more, so it sits at the boundary between complementarity and automation. The worker’s behavior is nearly the same in both, so it is the difference in AI capability between the two deployments that shifts the deployment from one regime to the other, as the framework predicts. The cost of undertrust is therefore uneven. We simulate a trust-calibrated decision rule, which recovers about 2.62.6 points accuracy for the strong AI and moves the team toward the boundary, but almost nothing for the weak AI.

β^=0.285\hat{\beta}=0.285

2.62.6

The two sides of the information-behavior divide provide two design levers. On the human side, trust should be set to the deployment’s accuracy-maximizing level, not reflexively to β^=1\hat{\beta}=1, since some undertrust is protective in the impairment region. On the AI side, reducing overlap by training the AI to supply what the human lacks rather than what she already knows can raise team accuracy even without raising the AI’s own accuracy. The phase diagram also says when to show the AI at all: withhold its signal when the AI is too weak, provide it in the complementarity band, and automate once the AI is strong enough.

β^=1\hat{\beta}=1

Our work sits among several literatures but differs in what it treats as endogenous. Studies of optimal human-AI collaboration through sufficient statistics ([Agarwal et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib3)) leave out the conditionally dependent signals that are central here. Work on reducing overreliance ([Buçinca et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib10)) and on testing whether AI adds to human expertise ([Alur et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib19); [Alur et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib20)) takes the intervention or the test as given, whereas we characterize the best deployment as a function of capability, overlap, and behavior. Closest in spirit, [Guo et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib21) define over- and under-reliance from the human’s adoption or switch rates against a Bayesian benchmark; our two parameters give a micro-foundation for their two sources of loss, trust for their reliance loss and correlation awareness for their discrimination loss, with a model of a worker who combines a continuous AI signal with her own rather than choosing per instance between the two recommendations. Other work on combining expert information ([Donahue et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib13); [Peng et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib14)) and learning-to-defer ([Madras et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib15); [Mozannar and Sontag, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib16); [Verma et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib17); [Wilder et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib18)) takes the human’s decision rule as exogenous, whereas we derive it from behavioral primitives. Section [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S2 "2 Model ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") introduces the model, Section [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3 "3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") develops the phase diagram and welfare decomposition, and Section [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S4 "4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") presents the empirical framework and results.

### 2.1 The Worker’s Decision Rule

After processing its cues, the AI communicates a sufficient statistic for ℓA\ell\_{A} to the human, such as a recommended answer, a probability report, or a textual explanation. We assume this communication is informationally equivalent to ℓA\ell\_{A} (the below analysis is agnostic to the format of the information). We refer to the human decision-maker who has communicated with AI and has access to (ℓH,ℓA)(\ell\_{H},\ell\_{A}) as the *worker*. The worker forms a posterior probability for Y=1Y=1 and provides a binary decision. We model the worker via two parameters that capture distinct primitives: one a belief about the joint distribution of signals, the other a behavioral discount on the AI’s contribution.

### 3.1 Performance Objective

The theorem yields several substantive insights that we elaborate below.

Insight 1: (Impairment Region) – A weak AI can hurt a worker who neglects correlation. The phase diagram has an *impairment* region where the worker assisted by the AI does worse than the worker alone (𝒜H​A<𝒜H\mathcal{A}\_{HA}<\mathcal{A}\_{H}). From Theorem [3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.Thmlemma2 "Theorem 3.2 (Phase diagram under correlation neglect). ‣ 3.2 Phase Diagram ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust"), this region exists whenever overlap satisfies λ>1−β^/2\lambda>1-\hat{\beta}/2. The mechanism is direct. When overlap is high, much of the AI’s evidence is content the worker already has. The correlation-neglect worker, using the rule ℓ^=ℓH+β^​ℓA\hat{\ell}=\ell\_{H}+\hat{\beta}\ell\_{A}, treats ℓA\ell\_{A} as if it were a fresh, independent signal. By giving ℓA\ell\_{A} full weight β^\hat{\beta}, she effectively double-counts the overlapping content. When the AI is weak (small τA\tau\_{A}), the genuinely new information in ℓA\ell\_{A} is too small to offset the double-counting penalty, and her accuracy falls below the human-alone benchmark.

The cue-pool interpretation imposes an upper bound τA≤τH/λ\tau\_{A}\leq\tau\_{H}/\lambda; at this boundary the AI’s evidence is Blackwell-equivalent to the team’s, so automation is welfare-optimal regardless of trust calibration. We instantiate the framework on ChatBench ([Chang et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib6)), a controlled MTurk study in which 643643 workers answer multiple-choice questions from MMLU ([Hendrycks et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#bib.bib5)) across math, physics, and moral reasoning. Trust calibration and design implications. Section [3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.SS3 "3.3 Welfare Decomposition ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust") splits the worker’s accuracy loss against the Bayes-rational benchmark into a correlation-neglect cost CNC\mathrm{CNC} and an undertrust cost UTC\mathrm{UTC}, with UTC\mathrm{UTC} the accuracy recovered by calibrating trust (Proposition [3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#S3.Thmlemma4 "Proposition 3.4 (Welfare decomposition). ‣ 3.3 Welfare Decomposition ‣ 3 Analysis ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")). Here, we measure the empirical counterpart of UTC\mathrm{UTC}. On items where the worker’s unaided answer and the AI’s recommendation disagree, we replace her final choice with a simulated trust-calibrated rule that selects whichever answer is more likely correct given the same two signals used to identify the behavioral parameters, her stated confidence ℓH\ell\_{H} and the AI’s question-level accuracy ℓA\ell\_{A}. Here, the correctness probabilities are estimated by cross-validated logistic regression (Appendix [K](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.05870v1#A11 "Appendix K Empirical welfare evaluation ‣ AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust")). Like UTC\mathrm{UTC}, the resulting gain isolates the trust channel: it changes how she relies on the AI. For GPT-4o, the simulated rule follows the AI on about 92%92\% of disagreements, versus the real workers’ 70%70\%, and raises team accuracy by 2.62.6 percentage points, from 0.8510.851 to 0.8770.877, close to the AI-alone accuracy of 0.8840.884. So for GPT-4o, which lies in the automation regime, calibrating trust moves the team nearly to the AI-alone benchmark. For Llama-3.1-8b, which sits at the complementarity-automation boundary, the simulated rule instead does worse than the actual workers (−1.4-1.4 percentage points). The reason is informational rather than behavioral: the simulated rule sees only two coarse signals, whereas the worker also reads the AI’s specific answer and can judge its reasoning, which for the weaker AI evidently outweighs calibrating trust. Two design implications follow from the result. First, trust calibration pays off more where the AI is strong, so interventions that raise trust should be targeted to AI-strong cases rather than applied uniformly. Meanwhile, besides behavior calibration, the granularity of information the worker receives is equally important.

Extensions to other applications. The contribution of our empirical framework extends beyond ChatBench’s setup with MMLU questions, and can be applied to other domains such as medicine, law, or programming, where human and AI expertise are combined. Estimating the model’s primitives requires only the observables present in any binary classification setting: the human-alone report ℓH\ell\_{H}, the AI-alone report ℓA\ell\_{A}, the AI-assisted human’s report ℓ^\hat{\ell}, and the ground-truth label YY.
